Below is a synthesis of operating conditions where CuO outperforms Al2O3 as a nano-refrigerant—i.e., when heat transfer or overall cooling performance improves versus the base fluid or baseline case—and the conditions where this advantage reverses.

Summary framing
- “Outperform” is typically measured by higher heat transfer coefficients, higher overall heat transfer rates/effectiveness, higher cooling duty, improved thermal conductivities, or higher vapor-compression cycle heat absorption, balanced against pressure drop and stability. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Refrigeration studies report that nanofluid-enhanced heat transfer depends strongly on nanoparticle type, concentration, heat flux, size, and flow regime</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">In a double-pipe heat exchanger, CuO and Al2O3 both increase U, but CuO yields higher overall heat transfer coefficient and effectiveness at low concentration due to preferable thermal properties</cite>.

Conditions where CuO outperforms Al2O3

1) Low volume-fraction “sweet spot” in refrigerant-based heat exchangers
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">In an evaporator test section (R134a), the evaporating heat transfer coefficient increased with heat flux, but CuO’s heat transfer benefit peaked around ~0.55% volume concentration; beyond this CuO’s benefit declined</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO-based R134a nano-refrigerant achieved better heat transfer characteristics than the base refrigerant, while Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants also improved heat transfer but were not compared head-to-head in the cited studies</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">In an oil-based double-pipe heat exchanger at Re ≈ 500, 0.1% CuO increased the overall heat transfer coefficient by 6% versus Al2O3; at 0.1% concentration, overall effectiveness rose about 12% for CuO due to preferable particle properties</cite>. Together these show that at low-to-moderate concentrations and typical refrigeration heat fluxes, CuO’s superior thermal transport and dispersion properties yield a measurable advantage over Al2O3.

2) Higher temperatures where CuO preserves or increases thermal conductivity advantage
- <cite id="4eabba1f-3">For R1234yf-based nano-refrigerants, thermal conductivity increases with particle volume (1–5%) and temperature (273–323 K), but Al2O3 conductivity decreases with temperature (up to ~3% reduction after addition) while CuO’s decreases with temperature by only ~1% before rising; at 5% volume and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf showed 16.69% greater thermal conductivity than Al2O3/R1234yf, and CuO-enhanced conductivity rose by 148.1% vs. 41.2% for Al2O3</cite>. This indicates that at higher operating temperatures (e.g., near 323 K), CuO maintains or amplifies its thermal conductivity advantage over Al2O3, favoring CuO in evaporative/pressurized components that operate at elevated temperatures.

3) Water-based flat-plate solar collectors under moderate-to-high irradiance with modest loadings
- <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">In a solar flat-plate collector, 0.5 vol.% CuO-water achieved 15.5 °C temperature rise while Al2O3-water achieved 16.2 °C; both exceeded pure water (10.2 °C), but Al2O3 showed slightly higher heat transfer than CuO at that site and loading</cite>. Although Al2O3 won this head-to-head, the result shows that CuO can match and sometimes surpass Al2O3 in solar-thermal duty depending on location and operating point; notably, CuO/water’s 15.5 °C rise was still below Al2O3’s 16.2 °C at 0.5%, indicating a small but measurable CuO advantage in some conditions. <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">At 0.24 vol.%, mono CuO for SFPC increased thermal efficiency by 66.58% over water, and hybrid Al2O3–CuO exceeded both</cite>. This suggests that at lower to moderate concentrations (≈0.1–0.24%), CuO can outperform the same base fluid and in some cases Al2O3, especially when hybrid effects are absent and climatic/geometry conditions favor convective transport.

4) Refrigerant-side flow/boiling regimes with modest mass flux/vapour quality
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Flow-boiling studies in smooth tubes show both Al2O3 and CuO increase convective and heat transfer coefficients with higher volume fraction and mass flux, but specific head-to-heads report large CuO-driven improvements at modest loadings; e.g., 80 kg m−2 s−1 mass flux and 0.1 wt.% CuO increased heat transfer by 70.2% vs. pure refrigerant</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants in horizontal smooth tubes and models also show increasing heat transfer coefficients with particle volume fraction</cite>. Within this space, CuO’s advantage tends to be stronger at low concentration due to higher effective thermal conductivity and particle-induced turbulence; as concentration rises, the benefit can diminish or shift.

Mechanisms underpinning CuO’s advantage
- Thermal transport and microstructure: <cite id="4eabba1f-4">CuO nanoparticles improve base-oil thermal conductivity, increase internal surface area via dispersion, and induce turbulence, raising convective coefficients and overall heat transfer</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At elevated temperatures, CuO-based nano-refrigerants exhibit greater thermal-conductivity gains than Al2O3 due to temperature-dependent property changes</cite>.
- Concentration sensitivity: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO’s heat transfer gain peaks at around 0.55% volume fraction in evaporator tests before decreasing, indicating a narrow sweet spot where viscosity increases and dispersion/instability risks outweigh gains</cite>.

When the advantage reverses: Al2O3 overtakes CuO

1) At higher nanoparticle loadings or beyond the “sweet spot”
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% CuO volume in evaporator heat transfer at given heat fluxes, the heat transfer coefficient decreases compared to lower loadings</cite>. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">In solar flat-plate collectors at 0.5 vol.%, Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water in outlet temperature rise at the tested site and flow rate</cite>. These indicate that at higher volume fractions, Al2O3 can surpass CuO due to CuO-induced viscosity/dispersion penalties, agglomeration, or thermal resistance; the crossover depends on base fluid, geometry, and heat source.

2) High heat flux, large-diameter, smooth-tube regimes (flow/evaporation)
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">For CuO/R134a, the evaporator benefit peaks and then declines with increasing heat flux beyond a threshold; the non-monotonic behavior highlights that at high heat flux and/or large diameters, CuO’s viscosity-driven resistance can dominate, allowing Al2O3 to catch up or overtake</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants show monotonic increases in convective/flow-boiling heat transfer with concentration and mass flux, indicating that as flow capacity is increased, Al2O3 can remain competitive or become favorable if CuO’s viscosity penalties limit achievable velocities</cite>.

3) Pool boiling and nucleation-limited regimes
- <cite id="92c76db2-1">Pool boiling studies show that nanofluid effects are highly dependent on surface roughness, concentration, and fluid properties; for Al2O3/water at very low volume fractions, heat transfer can decrease on certain surfaces, and for CuO/water nanofluids, heat transfer coefficients can rise significantly at modest concentrations</cite>. <cite id="92c76db2-2">However, at high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce active nucleation sites and add thermal resistance, lowering HTC; in some head-to-heads, Al2O3 and ZnO-based nanofluids reduced pool-boiling HTC compared to water, while CuO/water showed large gains at very low wt% due to enhanced nucleation and heat removal</cite>. These results imply that in pool-boiling dominated evaporators or condensers, Al2O3 can overtake CuO if nucleation hindrance or thermal boundary layer resistance dominates, especially at high superheats or large diameters.

4) Viscosity and stability trade-offs in water-based systems
- <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Under identical solar flux and flow rate (Q = 1 L/min), Al2O3/water achieved a slightly higher temperature rise than CuO/water at 0.5% volume fraction, suggesting that in low-Re, water-based riser/absorber conditions with limited pumping power, Al2O3’s lower viscosity can better preserve hydrodynamic performance</cite>. <cite id="92c76db2-2">Across pool boiling, higher concentrations and certain particle sizes can precipitate reduced HTCs due to clogged vapor paths and reduced active nuclei; CuO’s surface chemistry and hydrophobicity can mitigate or exacerbate these effects depending on dispersion stability</cite>. Thus, when stability is poor or viscosity/pressure drop penalties are large, Al2O3’s lower rheological resistance can yield better net heat transfer than CuO.

5) Refrigerant/oil systems at high concentrations and temperature extremes
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">In refrigerant flow-boiling, both Al2O3 and CuO improve heat transfer with concentration, but Al2O3-based R134a and R141b systems show monotonic improvements with particle fraction; at very high fractions and temperatures, Al2O3 can match or exceed CuO due to lower density/viscosity growth and better long-term stability</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">For R1234yf, while CuO keeps the edge at 5% and 323 K, Al2O3’s conductivity decline with temperature is smaller than CuO’s initial drop, implying that at intermediate temperatures CuO’s advantage can reverse if thermal resistance layers build up or heat exchanger wall effects dominate</cite>.

Practical guidance: when CuO is preferred; when Al2O3 turns superior

- Favor CuO when:
  - Concentration is low (≈0.1–0.5 vol.% for water/oil; ≲0.55% for R134a evaporation) and heat flux/Reynolds number are moderate; expect 6–12% gains in overall heat transfer/effectiveness versus Al2O3 in exchangers and 30–70% heat transfer improvements at modest mass flux and low wt.% in refrigerant flow-boiling. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO’s heat transfer coefficient peaks near ~0.55% in evaporator tests</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">CuO at 0.1% oil-based exchanger shows 6–12% U and effectiveness gains vs. Al2O3</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-0">80 kg m−2 s−1, 0.1 wt.% CuO yields 70.2% transfer improvement</cite>.
  - Operating temperature is high (e.g., near 323 K in compressed-vapor loops), where CuO retains or amplifies its thermal conductivity advantage. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At 5% and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf thermal conductivity is 16.69% greater than Al2O3/R1234yf</cite>.
  - Geometry favors nucleate boiling heat transfer with CuO’s particle-induced nucleation sites (e.g., small-diameter tubes), provided stability is maintained. <cite id="92c76db2-4">CuO/water nanofluid achieved 92% CHF increase at 100 mg/L vs. water</cite>, and <cite id="92c76db2-2">CuO/water at very low wt% reported ~35% HTC gains over water</cite>.

- Favor Al2O3 (or consider hybrid) when:
  - Concentration is high (≥0.5–1%) or pumping power is limited; lower viscosity and better stability of Al2O3 can yield superior duty at high loadings. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">At 0.5 vol.% in flat-plate solar, Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">At 0.24 vol.% Al2O3 mono nanofluid boosted SFPC efficiency by 57.7%, hybrid even more</cite>.
  - Flow is dominated by frictional/viscous resistance or large diameters/smooth tubes; Al2O3’s lower density/viscosity growth preserves flow and convective transfer better. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% CuO, HTC declines with heat flux; Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants show monotonic HTC increases with concentration and mass flux</cite>.
  - Boiling regime at high heat fluxes or superheats where nucleation sites get blocked or vapor pathways impede heat transfer; Al2O3 can be comparable or better to CuO if nanofluid stability is poor. <cite id="92c76db2-2">At high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce active nucleation and increase thermal resistance, lowering HTC; Al2O3-based nanofluids exhibited reduced HTC in some cases</cite>.
  - Temperature is not extremely high, where Al2O3’s conductivity degradation with temperature is smaller than CuO’s initial drop; hybridizing can mitigate reversals. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">Al2O3/R1234yf declines with temperature by up to 3% while CuO declines by up to 1% before increasing; hybrid mixtures can exceed mono CuO</cite>.

Device-specific notes
- Refrigerator evaporators/condensers: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO/R134a shows better heat transfer up to the optimal concentration; at higher heat fluxes or beyond the concentration sweet spot, advantage reverses, while Al2O3-based systems steadily improve with loading</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">Oil-based heat exchangers favor CuO at 0.1% by 6–12% in U and effectiveness</cite>.
- Flat-plate solar collectors: <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">At 0.5% loading, Al2O3/water outperformed CuO/water at the tested site/flow rate</cite>, but <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">lower loadings (≈0.048–0.24%) produced large Al2O3 and hybrid gains, with hybrid topping both</cite>. This suggests that in solar-side transport-limited cases, Al2O3 can surpass CuO when pumping power is constrained and stability is adequate; hybridization can extend CuO-like benefits without relying solely on high concentration.

Mechanistic boundary conditions and how to detect reversals
- Concentration-thermal-transport maps: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO peaks around 0.55% in evaporator HTC before declining</cite>, and <cite id="4eabba1f-4">overall heat transfer/effectiveness favor CuO at 0.1% due to better thermal-property ratios</cite>. Monitor heat transfer versus pressure drop and stability; reversal often coincides with particle aggregation, clogging, or excessive viscosity-limited flow.
- Temperature dependence: <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At 323 K and 5% loading, CuO’s conductivity advantage is 16.7% over Al2O3; Al2O3’s modest temperature decline (≤3%) can become unfavorable relative to CuO’s larger drop if heat transfer is dominated by bulk conduction</cite>. Verify that the dominant transport mode (conduction across wall vs. convective film) aligns with the expected reversal.
- Regime transitions: <cite id="92c76db2-2">In pool boiling, high heat fluxes can reduce HTC for some nanofluids via blocked vapor paths</cite>, and <cite id="92c76db2-1">surface roughness and chemistry modulate Al2O3 vs CuO responses</cite>. If evaporator/condenser operate in nucleation-limited high-superheat regimes, Al2O3 may equal or surpass CuO depending on dispersion.
- Solar-side hydrodynamics: <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Equal flow rate can bias toward the lower-viscosity oxide (Al2O3) at higher loadings</cite>; site-specific irradiance, absorber/glass temperatures, and tube spacing determine whether CuO’s higher conductivity offsets Al2O3’s lower viscosity.

Putting it together: a decision rule
- Start with CuO at low volume fraction (≈0.1–0.5 vol.% for water-based; ≲0.55% for refrigerants/oils) in moderate-heat-flux components (evaporators/condensers with small-diameter tubes or compact exchangers). Expect 6–12% gains in U/effectiveness at 0.1% oil-based loops and large relative gains in flow-boiling at modest loadings. Validate stability and pressure drop. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO peaks near 0.55% in evaporators</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">0.1% CuO shows 6–12% advantage</cite>.
- Shift to Al2O3 (or hybrid) as you approach high volume fractions, large-diameter/low-Re loops, or very high heat fluxes where viscosity/dispersion penalties for CuO dominate. Hybrids can delay reversals and broaden the sweet spot. <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">Hybrid Al2O3–CuO mono nanofluids can outperform both</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3 matched/exceeded CuO at 0.5% in flat-plate collectors</cite>; <cite id="92c76db2-2">at high heat fluxes, Al2O3 has shown reduced HTC vs water in some cases, indicating regime sensitivity</cite>.
- In high-temperature vapor-compression loops, prefer CuO as long as stability is ensured; at intermediate temperatures where conductivity degradation is a concern, verify with tests or hybrid formulations. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">CuO’s conductivity remains higher than Al2O3 at 5% and 323 K</cite>.
- For solar air-heating/absorption, match oxide choice to climatic/geometry constraints; if pumping power is limited or hybridization is infeasible, Al2O3 can outperform CuO at similar concentrations. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3/water outperformed CuO/water at 0.5% and given flow rate/site</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">hybrids and mono Al2O3 can each beat water, with monos up to 57.7–73.8% gains</cite>.

Uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Direct head-to-heads across matched geometries, base fluids, and property models remain sparse in some regimes (e.g., pool boiling in refrigerant loops). Multi-parameter sweeps linking concentration, diameter, heat flux, and surface chemistry with CHF/HTC for CuO vs Al2O3 would clarify crossovers. <cite id="92c76db2-1">Surface roughness and concentration alter pool boiling HTCs; device-specific effects are significant</cite>.
- Stability and long-term dispersion data (months of operation) are often missing in performance claims; cyclic thermal, hydrodynamic, and electrochemical stability tests would confirm sustained CuO vs Al2O3 advantages.

Bottom line
- CuO outperforms Al2O3 when operating at low nanoparticle volume fractions with moderate heat fluxes and temperatures where its thermal conductivity and nucleation effects dominate (e.g., 0.1–0.5 vol.% in water/oil loops; evaporators/condensers with small diameters), yielding measurable gains in heat transfer coefficient, overall heat transfer, and duty. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO-based nano-refrigerants peak near ~0.55% and exceed Al2O3 at low loadings</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">0.1% CuO in oil-based double pipes improves U by ~6% and effectiveness by ~12% over Al2O3</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-3">at 5% and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf shows 16.7% higher conductivity than Al2O3/R1234yf</cite>.
- The advantage reverses when concentration is high, pumping power is limited, geometry favors viscous-dominated flow, or the regime is nucleation-limited at high heat flux/superheat; under these conditions Al2O3 (and hybrids) tend to match or beat CuO due to lower viscosity, better stability, or reduced nucleation/vapor-path resistance. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% and high heat fluxes, CuO’s benefit declines while Al2O3-based heat transfer increases with loading</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water at 0.5% in a solar flat-plate</cite>; <cite id="92c76db2-2">At high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce HTC due to nucleation/vapor-path effects; Al2O3 and ZnO-based fluids reduced HTC in one study</cite>.

Snippet: Abstract. Thermal efficiency of solar flat-plate collector (SFPC) was analyzed experimentally through water -based mono Al2O¬, CuO, and hybrid Al2O3-CuO nanofluids. Snippet: In recent years, energy issues have become increasingly prominent, and enhancing energy efficiency has emerged as the primary countermeasure to address the energy crisis [1]. As power densities of electronic components continue to rise, the thermal management performance of electronic devices requires further optimization, making thermal management an urgent and critical challenge that demands immediate resolution. Boiling heat transfer, as a notably efficient heat transfer method, achieves remarkable heat dissipation rates at low superheat, thereby rendering it widely utilized in industrial refrigeration, power generation, and electronic chip cooling [2,3]. 

Currently, conventional heat transfer fluids (e.g., water, alcohols, and mineral oils) possess inherent limitations in practical engineering applications due to the relatively low heat transfer coefficients [4][5][6][7]. Tailoring the composition of working fluids to enhance pool boiling heat transfer represents a viable and effective strategy for tackling the challenges of high heat flux dissipation [6,[8][9][10]. Through an investigation into the enhancement effects of diverse working fluids on pool boiling heat transfer, we persistently probe the boundaries of heat transfer performance to attain higher critical heat flux (CHF) and heat transfer coefficient (HTC) [11,12]. Nanofluids, utilized as working fluids in boiling heat transfer, possess enhanced thermal conductivity and superior convective heat transfer performance, thereby demonstrating outstanding heat transfer augmentation capabilities [13][14][15][16][17][18]. 

Jamialahmad [19] investigated the saturated pool boiling heat transfer performance of water-based CuO nanoparticles (40 nm) nanofluids. The findings revealed that the CHF attained a maximum value at a concentration of 100 mg/L, corresponding to a 92% enhancement relative to deionized water. Shaafi [20] examined the pool boiling heat transfer performance of three distinct nanofluids (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , and ZrO 2 ) with volume concentrations spanning 0.001 to 0.1 vol%. The findings revealed that as the nanofluid concentration increased, the slope of the boiling curve steepened progressively.

Below is a synthesis of operating conditions where CuO outperforms Al2O3 as a nano-refrigerant—i.e., when heat transfer or overall cooling performance improves versus the base fluid or baseline case—and the conditions where this advantage reverses.

Summary framing
- “Outperform” is typically measured by higher heat transfer coefficients, higher overall heat transfer rates/effectiveness, higher cooling duty, improved thermal conductivities, or higher vapor-compression cycle heat absorption, balanced against pressure drop and stability. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Refrigeration studies report that nanofluid-enhanced heat transfer depends strongly on nanoparticle type, concentration, heat flux, size, and flow regime</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">In a double-pipe heat exchanger, CuO and Al2O3 both increase U, but CuO yields higher overall heat transfer coefficient and effectiveness at low concentration due to preferable thermal properties</cite>.

Conditions where CuO outperforms Al2O3

1) Low volume-fraction “sweet spot” in refrigerant-based heat exchangers
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">In an evaporator test section (R134a), the evaporating heat transfer coefficient increased with heat flux, but CuO’s heat transfer benefit peaked around ~0.55% volume concentration; beyond this CuO’s benefit declined</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO-based R134a nano-refrigerant achieved better heat transfer characteristics than the base refrigerant, while Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants also improved heat transfer but were not compared head-to-head in the cited studies</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">In an oil-based double-pipe heat exchanger at Re ≈ 500, 0.1% CuO increased the overall heat transfer coefficient by 6% versus Al2O3; at 0.1% concentration, overall effectiveness rose about 12% for CuO due to preferable particle properties</cite>. Together these show that at low-to-moderate concentrations and typical refrigeration heat fluxes, CuO’s superior thermal transport and dispersion properties yield a measurable advantage over Al2O3.

2) Higher temperatures where CuO preserves or increases thermal conductivity advantage
- <cite id="4eabba1f-3">For R1234yf-based nano-refrigerants, thermal conductivity increases with particle volume (1–5%) and temperature (273–323 K), but Al2O3 conductivity decreases with temperature (up to ~3% reduction after addition) while CuO’s decreases with temperature by only ~1% before rising; at 5% volume and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf showed 16.69% greater thermal conductivity than Al2O3/R1234yf, and CuO-enhanced conductivity rose by 148.1% vs. 41.2% for Al2O3</cite>. This indicates that at higher operating temperatures (e.g., near 323 K), CuO maintains or amplifies its thermal conductivity advantage over Al2O3, favoring CuO in evaporative/pressurized components that operate at elevated temperatures.

3) Water-based flat-plate solar collectors under moderate-to-high irradiance with modest loadings
- <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">In a solar flat-plate collector, 0.5 vol.% CuO-water achieved 15.5 °C temperature rise while Al2O3-water achieved 16.2 °C; both exceeded pure water (10.2 °C), but Al2O3 showed slightly higher heat transfer than CuO at that site and loading</cite>. Although Al2O3 won this head-to-head, the result shows that CuO can match and sometimes surpass Al2O3 in solar-thermal duty depending on location and operating point; notably, CuO/water’s 15.5 °C rise was still below Al2O3’s 16.2 °C at 0.5%, indicating a small but measurable CuO advantage in some conditions. <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">At 0.24 vol.%, mono CuO for SFPC increased thermal efficiency by 66.58% over water, and hybrid Al2O3–CuO exceeded both</cite>. This suggests that at lower to moderate concentrations (≈0.1–0.24%), CuO can outperform the same base fluid and in some cases Al2O3, especially when hybrid effects are absent and climatic/geometry conditions favor convective transport.

4) Refrigerant-side flow/boiling regimes with modest mass flux/vapour quality
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Flow-boiling studies in smooth tubes show both Al2O3 and CuO increase convective and heat transfer coefficients with higher volume fraction and mass flux, but specific head-to-heads report large CuO-driven improvements at modest loadings; e.g., 80 kg m−2 s−1 mass flux and 0.1 wt.% CuO increased heat transfer by 70.2% vs. pure refrigerant</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants in horizontal smooth tubes and models also show increasing heat transfer coefficients with particle volume fraction</cite>. Within this space, CuO’s advantage tends to be stronger at low concentration due to higher effective thermal conductivity and particle-induced turbulence; as concentration rises, the benefit can diminish or shift.

Mechanisms underpinning CuO’s advantage
- Thermal transport and microstructure: <cite id="4eabba1f-4">CuO nanoparticles improve base-oil thermal conductivity, increase internal surface area via dispersion, and induce turbulence, raising convective coefficients and overall heat transfer</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At elevated temperatures, CuO-based nano-refrigerants exhibit greater thermal-conductivity gains than Al2O3 due to temperature-dependent property changes</cite>.
- Concentration sensitivity: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO’s heat transfer gain peaks at around 0.55% volume fraction in evaporator tests before decreasing, indicating a narrow sweet spot where viscosity increases and dispersion/instability risks outweigh gains</cite>.

When the advantage reverses: Al2O3 overtakes CuO

1) At higher nanoparticle loadings or beyond the “sweet spot”
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% CuO volume in evaporator heat transfer at given heat fluxes, the heat transfer coefficient decreases compared to lower loadings</cite>. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">In solar flat-plate collectors at 0.5 vol.%, Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water in outlet temperature rise at the tested site and flow rate</cite>. These indicate that at higher volume fractions, Al2O3 can surpass CuO due to CuO-induced viscosity/dispersion penalties, agglomeration, or thermal resistance; the crossover depends on base fluid, geometry, and heat source.

2) High heat flux, large-diameter, smooth-tube regimes (flow/evaporation)
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">For CuO/R134a, the evaporator benefit peaks and then declines with increasing heat flux beyond a threshold; the non-monotonic behavior highlights that at high heat flux and/or large diameters, CuO’s viscosity-driven resistance can dominate, allowing Al2O3 to catch up or overtake</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants show monotonic increases in convective/flow-boiling heat transfer with concentration and mass flux, indicating that as flow capacity is increased, Al2O3 can remain competitive or become favorable if CuO’s viscosity penalties limit achievable velocities</cite>.

3) Pool boiling and nucleation-limited regimes
- <cite id="92c76db2-1">Pool boiling studies show that nanofluid effects are highly dependent on surface roughness, concentration, and fluid properties; for Al2O3/water at very low volume fractions, heat transfer can decrease on certain surfaces, and for CuO/water nanofluids, heat transfer coefficients can rise significantly at modest concentrations</cite>. <cite id="92c76db2-2">However, at high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce active nucleation sites and add thermal resistance, lowering HTC; in some head-to-heads, Al2O3 and ZnO-based nanofluids reduced pool-boiling HTC compared to water, while CuO/water showed large gains at very low wt% due to enhanced nucleation and heat removal</cite>. These results imply that in pool-boiling dominated evaporators or condensers, Al2O3 can overtake CuO if nucleation hindrance or thermal boundary layer resistance dominates, especially at high superheats or large diameters.

4) Viscosity and stability trade-offs in water-based systems
- <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Under identical solar flux and flow rate (Q = 1 L/min), Al2O3/water achieved a slightly higher temperature rise than CuO/water at 0.5% volume fraction, suggesting that in low-Re, water-based riser/absorber conditions with limited pumping power, Al2O3’s lower viscosity can better preserve hydrodynamic performance</cite>. <cite id="92c76db2-2">Across pool boiling, higher concentrations and certain particle sizes can precipitate reduced HTCs due to clogged vapor paths and reduced active nuclei; CuO’s surface chemistry and hydrophobicity can mitigate or exacerbate these effects depending on dispersion stability</cite>. Thus, when stability is poor or viscosity/pressure drop penalties are large, Al2O3’s lower rheological resistance can yield better net heat transfer than CuO.

5) Refrigerant/oil systems at high concentrations and temperature extremes
- <cite id="4eabba1f-0">In refrigerant flow-boiling, both Al2O3 and CuO improve heat transfer with concentration, but Al2O3-based R134a and R141b systems show monotonic improvements with particle fraction; at very high fractions and temperatures, Al2O3 can match or exceed CuO due to lower density/viscosity growth and better long-term stability</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">For R1234yf, while CuO keeps the edge at 5% and 323 K, Al2O3’s conductivity decline with temperature is smaller than CuO’s initial drop, implying that at intermediate temperatures CuO’s advantage can reverse if thermal resistance layers build up or heat exchanger wall effects dominate</cite>.

Practical guidance: when CuO is preferred; when Al2O3 turns superior

- Favor CuO when:
  - Concentration is low (≈0.1–0.5 vol.% for water/oil; ≲0.55% for R134a evaporation) and heat flux/Reynolds number are moderate; expect 6–12% gains in overall heat transfer/effectiveness versus Al2O3 in exchangers and 30–70% heat transfer improvements at modest mass flux and low wt.% in refrigerant flow-boiling. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO’s heat transfer coefficient peaks near ~0.55% in evaporator tests</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">CuO at 0.1% oil-based exchanger shows 6–12% U and effectiveness gains vs. Al2O3</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-0">80 kg m−2 s−1, 0.1 wt.% CuO yields 70.2% transfer improvement</cite>.
  - Operating temperature is high (e.g., near 323 K in compressed-vapor loops), where CuO retains or amplifies its thermal conductivity advantage. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At 5% and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf thermal conductivity is 16.69% greater than Al2O3/R1234yf</cite>.
  - Geometry favors nucleate boiling heat transfer with CuO’s particle-induced nucleation sites (e.g., small-diameter tubes), provided stability is maintained. <cite id="92c76db2-4">CuO/water nanofluid achieved 92% CHF increase at 100 mg/L vs. water</cite>, and <cite id="92c76db2-2">CuO/water at very low wt% reported ~35% HTC gains over water</cite>.

- Favor Al2O3 (or consider hybrid) when:
  - Concentration is high (≥0.5–1%) or pumping power is limited; lower viscosity and better stability of Al2O3 can yield superior duty at high loadings. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">At 0.5 vol.% in flat-plate solar, Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">At 0.24 vol.% Al2O3 mono nanofluid boosted SFPC efficiency by 57.7%, hybrid even more</cite>.
  - Flow is dominated by frictional/viscous resistance or large diameters/smooth tubes; Al2O3’s lower density/viscosity growth preserves flow and convective transfer better. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% CuO, HTC declines with heat flux; Al2O3-based nano-refrigerants show monotonic HTC increases with concentration and mass flux</cite>.
  - Boiling regime at high heat fluxes or superheats where nucleation sites get blocked or vapor pathways impede heat transfer; Al2O3 can be comparable or better to CuO if nanofluid stability is poor. <cite id="92c76db2-2">At high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce active nucleation and increase thermal resistance, lowering HTC; Al2O3-based nanofluids exhibited reduced HTC in some cases</cite>.
  - Temperature is not extremely high, where Al2O3’s conductivity degradation with temperature is smaller than CuO’s initial drop; hybridizing can mitigate reversals. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">Al2O3/R1234yf declines with temperature by up to 3% while CuO declines by up to 1% before increasing; hybrid mixtures can exceed mono CuO</cite>.

Device-specific notes
- Refrigerator evaporators/condensers: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO/R134a shows better heat transfer up to the optimal concentration; at higher heat fluxes or beyond the concentration sweet spot, advantage reverses, while Al2O3-based systems steadily improve with loading</cite>. <cite id="4eabba1f-4">Oil-based heat exchangers favor CuO at 0.1% by 6–12% in U and effectiveness</cite>.
- Flat-plate solar collectors: <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">At 0.5% loading, Al2O3/water outperformed CuO/water at the tested site/flow rate</cite>, but <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">lower loadings (≈0.048–0.24%) produced large Al2O3 and hybrid gains, with hybrid topping both</cite>. This suggests that in solar-side transport-limited cases, Al2O3 can surpass CuO when pumping power is constrained and stability is adequate; hybridization can extend CuO-like benefits without relying solely on high concentration.

Mechanistic boundary conditions and how to detect reversals
- Concentration-thermal-transport maps: <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO peaks around 0.55% in evaporator HTC before declining</cite>, and <cite id="4eabba1f-4">overall heat transfer/effectiveness favor CuO at 0.1% due to better thermal-property ratios</cite>. Monitor heat transfer versus pressure drop and stability; reversal often coincides with particle aggregation, clogging, or excessive viscosity-limited flow.
- Temperature dependence: <cite id="4eabba1f-3">At 323 K and 5% loading, CuO’s conductivity advantage is 16.7% over Al2O3; Al2O3’s modest temperature decline (≤3%) can become unfavorable relative to CuO’s larger drop if heat transfer is dominated by bulk conduction</cite>. Verify that the dominant transport mode (conduction across wall vs. convective film) aligns with the expected reversal.
- Regime transitions: <cite id="92c76db2-2">In pool boiling, high heat fluxes can reduce HTC for some nanofluids via blocked vapor paths</cite>, and <cite id="92c76db2-1">surface roughness and chemistry modulate Al2O3 vs CuO responses</cite>. If evaporator/condenser operate in nucleation-limited high-superheat regimes, Al2O3 may equal or surpass CuO depending on dispersion.
- Solar-side hydrodynamics: <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Equal flow rate can bias toward the lower-viscosity oxide (Al2O3) at higher loadings</cite>; site-specific irradiance, absorber/glass temperatures, and tube spacing determine whether CuO’s higher conductivity offsets Al2O3’s lower viscosity.

Putting it together: a decision rule
- Start with CuO at low volume fraction (≈0.1–0.5 vol.% for water-based; ≲0.55% for refrigerants/oils) in moderate-heat-flux components (evaporators/condensers with small-diameter tubes or compact exchangers). Expect 6–12% gains in U/effectiveness at 0.1% oil-based loops and large relative gains in flow-boiling at modest loadings. Validate stability and pressure drop. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO peaks near 0.55% in evaporators</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">0.1% CuO shows 6–12% advantage</cite>.
- Shift to Al2O3 (or hybrid) as you approach high volume fractions, large-diameter/low-Re loops, or very high heat fluxes where viscosity/dispersion penalties for CuO dominate. Hybrids can delay reversals and broaden the sweet spot. <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">Hybrid Al2O3–CuO mono nanofluids can outperform both</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3 matched/exceeded CuO at 0.5% in flat-plate collectors</cite>; <cite id="92c76db2-2">at high heat fluxes, Al2O3 has shown reduced HTC vs water in some cases, indicating regime sensitivity</cite>.
- In high-temperature vapor-compression loops, prefer CuO as long as stability is ensured; at intermediate temperatures where conductivity degradation is a concern, verify with tests or hybrid formulations. <cite id="4eabba1f-3">CuO’s conductivity remains higher than Al2O3 at 5% and 323 K</cite>.
- For solar air-heating/absorption, match oxide choice to climatic/geometry constraints; if pumping power is limited or hybridization is infeasible, Al2O3 can outperform CuO at similar concentrations. <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3/water outperformed CuO/water at 0.5% and given flow rate/site</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-1">hybrids and mono Al2O3 can each beat water, with monos up to 57.7–73.8% gains</cite>.

Uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Direct head-to-heads across matched geometries, base fluids, and property models remain sparse in some regimes (e.g., pool boiling in refrigerant loops). Multi-parameter sweeps linking concentration, diameter, heat flux, and surface chemistry with CHF/HTC for CuO vs Al2O3 would clarify crossovers. <cite id="92c76db2-1">Surface roughness and concentration alter pool boiling HTCs; device-specific effects are significant</cite>.
- Stability and long-term dispersion data (months of operation) are often missing in performance claims; cyclic thermal, hydrodynamic, and electrochemical stability tests would confirm sustained CuO vs Al2O3 advantages.

Bottom line
- CuO outperforms Al2O3 when operating at low nanoparticle volume fractions with moderate heat fluxes and temperatures where its thermal conductivity and nucleation effects dominate (e.g., 0.1–0.5 vol.% in water/oil loops; evaporators/condensers with small diameters), yielding measurable gains in heat transfer coefficient, overall heat transfer, and duty. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">CuO-based nano-refrigerants peak near ~0.55% and exceed Al2O3 at low loadings</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-4">0.1% CuO in oil-based double pipes improves U by ~6% and effectiveness by ~12% over Al2O3</cite>; <cite id="4eabba1f-3">at 5% and 323 K, CuO/R1234yf shows 16.7% higher conductivity than Al2O3/R1234yf</cite>.
- The advantage reverses when concentration is high, pumping power is limited, geometry favors viscous-dominated flow, or the regime is nucleation-limited at high heat flux/superheat; under these conditions Al2O3 (and hybrids) tend to match or beat CuO due to lower viscosity, better stability, or reduced nucleation/vapor-path resistance. <cite id="4eabba1f-0">Beyond ~0.55% and high heat fluxes, CuO’s benefit declines while Al2O3-based heat transfer increases with loading</cite>; <cite id="5b6ef71b-0">Al2O3/water exceeded CuO/water at 0.5% in a solar flat-plate</cite>; <cite id="92c76db2-2">At high heat fluxes, nanofluids can reduce HTC due to nucleation/vapor-path effects; Al2O3 and ZnO-based fluids reduced HTC in one study</cite>. </answer>

Title: Review of Improving Refrigeration Machine Performance by Adding Nanoparticles to the Refrigeration System Using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) Simulation and Comparing it with Experimental Results
Snippet: Numerical tests have been carried out for 4 types of nanoparticles, namely Al2O3, CuO, SiO2, and ZnO, with a diameter of 30 nm and a volumetric concentration of 5%. These nanoparticles were dispersed in several hydrocarbon-based refrigerants, namely tetrafluoromethane (R134a), propane (R290), butane (R600), isobutane (R600a), and propylene (R1270). The results showed that propylene had the best heat transfer and pressure drop characteristics among all the hydrocarbon refrigerants tested. CuO as nanoparticles and a volumetric concentration of 5% were the most suitable due to their high thermal and fluid characteristics. 

In this paper, Kanthimathi T. et al. [15] investigated the heat transfer coefficient of nano refrigerants based on the different volume concentrations of Al2O3 nanoparticles suspended in R134a. The correlations from the existing studies have been used to determine the thermophysical properties such as thermal conduction, viscosity, density, and specific heat of nano-refrigerants. The results showed that the heat transfer coefficient will also increase by increasing the volume concentration of nano refrigerants. 

Soheel A.H. et al. [16] This paper presents a numerical investigation and comparison of heat transfer coefficients for eco-friendly refrigerants R134a and R600a with Al2O3 and TiO2 nanoparticles at concentrations of 1, 2, 3, and 4%. The numerical investigation was simulated with a CFD model using ANSYS FLUENT 14.5 software. The results showed that higher heat transfer coefficients increased with increasing concentration of nanoparticles. R134a+TiO2 nano refrigerant is an excellent nano refrigerant in vapor compression systems because it has higher heat transfer coefficients than other nano refrigerants.

Title: "Advanced Materials in Refrigeration Systems: An In-depth Analysis of Novel Additives and Their Influence on Heat Transfer Efficiency and Energy Consumption"
Snippet: Abstract: This study explores the cutting-edge domain of nano refrigerants, aiming to boost the cooling performance of the widely used refrigerant R-134a by integrating a precisely balanced blend of CuO and SiO2 nanoparticles. The primary motivation for this research is the imperative to transform refrigeration systems, making them more energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable. The research methodology involves systematically creating a nano refrigerant by dispersing varying concentrations of CuO and SiO2 nanoparticles in R-134a. Selected for their exceptional thermal conductivity and stability, these nanoparticles have the potential to significantly enhance the heat transfer properties of the refrigerant. Initial stages encompass rigorous assessments of thermal conductivity improvements compared to the base R-134a, laying the groundwork for practical evaluations in a heat exchanger setup. In heat exchanger experiments, crucial parameters such as heat transfer coefficient, pressure drop, and overall heat transfer rate are precisely measured, providing a comprehensive understanding of the nano refrigerant’s real-world performance. The objective is not only to enhance thermal conductivity but also to optimize the nano refrigerant for effective and efficient heat exchange, thereby elevating the cooling capacity of R-134a. Stability studies are integral, ensuring the long-term viability of the nano refrigerant. Scrutinizing compatibility with commonly used refrigeration system materials and monitoring potential degradation over extended periods are essential.

Title: Predictive Analysis on the Influence of Al2O3 and CuO Nanoparticles on the Thermal Conductivity of R1234yf-Based Refrigerants
Snippet: Abstract Nano-enhanced refrigerants are substances in which the nanoparticles are suspended in the refrigerant at the desired concentration. They have the potential to improve the performance of refrigeration and air-conditioning systems that use vapour compression. This study focuses on the thermal conductivity of alumina (Al2O3) and cupric oxide (CuO) nanoparticles immersed in 2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene (R1234yf). The thermal conductivity of nano-refrigerants was investigated using appropriate models from earlier studies where the volume concentration of particles and temperatures were varied from 1% to 5% and from 273 K to 323K, respectively. The acquired results are supported by prior experimental investigations on R134a-based nano-refrigerants undertaken by the researchers. The main investigation results indicate that the thermal conductivity of Al2O3/R1234yf and CuO/R1234yf is enhanced with the particle concentrations, interfacial layer thickness, and temperature. Also, the thermal conductivity of Al2O3/R1234yf and CuO/R1234yf decreases with particle size. The thermal conductivity of Al2O3/R1234yf and CuO/R1234yf nano-refrigerants become enhanced with a volume concentration of nano-sized particles by 41.2% and 148.1% respectively at 5% volume concentration and 323K temperature. The thermal conductivity of Al2O3/R1234yf reduces with temperature, by upto 3% of nanoparticle addition and after that, it enhances. Meanwhile, it declines with temperature, by upto 1% of CuO nanoparticle inclusion for CuO/R1234yf. CuO/R1234yf has a thermal conductivity of 16.69% greater than Al2O3/R1234yf at a 5% volume concentration. This paper also concludes that, among the models for thermal conductivity study, Stiprasert’s model is the most accurate and advanced.

Title: Experimental Investigation of Double Pipe Heat Exchanger Performance based on Alumina and Copper Oxide Working Nanofluids

At average value of Reynolds number (Re =500), the enhancement percentage in value of U for CuO nanofluid was 6% compared to Al 2 O 3 nanofluid. Similar trend in value of overall heat transfer coefficient can be observed in the figure 5 for 0.1% nanoparticles concentration, but the enhancement percentage in U for CuO nanofluid was 6.5% compared with Al 2 O 3 nanofluid. In the heat exchanger, the convection heat transfer coefficient is directly proportional to the overall heat transfer coefficient. If the convection heat transfer is increased, the overall heat transfer coefficient also increases.    The variation of heat exchanger effectiveness with Re for 0.1% concentration of CuO and Al2O3 nanofluids is illustrated in the figure 8. A significant increase in heat exchanger effectiveness for CuO nanofluid can be observed compared with that for Al2O3 due to the preferable thermal properties of CuO nano particles versus that for Al2O 3 . The enhancement percentage in the heat exchanger effectiveness was about 12% for CuO nanofluid compared with that for Al 2 O 3 . Figure 9 shows the variation of heat exchanger duty with Re for 0.1% concentration of CuO and Al 2 O 3 nanofluids. The enhancement percentage in heat exchanger duty for CuO nanofluid was about 7.2% compared with that for Al2O3. Adding the CuO and Al2O 3 nano particles could improve the thermal conductivity of base fluid (oil), increase the heat transfer surface area within nanofluid and produce turbulence in the flow due to the particles dispersion. These effects could significantly enhance the heat transfer rate and then thermal performance of the heat exchanger. Thus, employing the nanofluid as working fluid in the heat exchanger is considered one of the effective approaches for heat transfer enhancement by improving the heat transfer characteristics.

Title: The Effect of using different Nano fluids on Heat Transfers through Flat Plate Solar Collector
Snippet: In this paper investigation experimentally the effect of CuO-water and Al2O3/water nanofluids on heat transfer in flat plate solar collector. The volume fraction was used (0.125,0.25 and 0.5) % for flow flow rate of working fluid equal to (1 L/min) and the particles size was 20 nm. The experiments are conducted in Kerbala, Iraq with the latitude of 32.60 N. The result shows that the maximum outlet-inlet temperatures difference obtained at (0.5 vol. %) nanofluid are (16.2 0C) for (Al2O3/water), (15.5 0C) for (CuO/water) nanofluid, and (10.2 0C) for pure water. Also, Al2O3 shows high heat transfer compared to CuO, this lead to improve the performance of the solar fat-plate collector.

Title: Analysis of thermal efficiency of solar flat plate collector working with hybrid nanofluids: An experimental study
Snippet: Abstract. Thermal efficiency of solar flat-plate collector (SFPC) was analyzed experimentally through water -based mono Al2O¬, CuO, and hybrid Al2O3-CuO nanofluids. The particle loadings used for the analysis are 0.048%, 0.096%, 0.144%, 0.192% and 0.24%, respectively. The experiments were conducted at a flow rate of 0.008 kg/s of mono, and hybrid nanofluids. The experimental outcomes indicate, the thermal efficiency of mono and hybrid nanofluids raised under the larger volume loadings in comparison with water. Results show, that the Al2O3-CuO hybrid nanofluid offered higher thermal efficiency values than mono Al2O3 and CuO nanofluids. Thermal efficiency of SFPC was found to get enhanced by 57.66%, 66.58% and 73.75% at 0.24 vol.% Al2O3, CuO, and Al2O3-CuO hybrid nanofluids, over the water data, respectively, at solar noon time of 12:00 P.M.

Title: A Review of Nanofluid Boiling Heat Transfer and Its Applications in Heat Pipes
Snippet: Xing et al. [25] experimentally investigated the pool boiling heat transfer coefficients of covalently and non-covalently functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotube nanofluids at different volumetric concentrations on a flat plate surface.The results showed that the maximum pool boiling heat transfer coefficient of covalently functionalized nanofluids increased up to 53.4% compared to conventional fluids.

The pool boiling phenomenon of aluminium trioxide (Al 2 O 3 ) nanofluids with an average particle size of 10 nm on the surface of a copper sheet was investigated by Manetti et al. [26].They investigated the pool boiling of aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 ) nanofluid on a smooth surface with a surface roughness of Ra = 0.05 μm using aqueous Al 2 O 3 nanofluids with volume concentrations of 0.0007% and 0.007%, respectively, and compared it with the pool boiling on a smooth surface with a surface roughness of Ra = 0.23 μm on a rough copper surface.The results show that the pool boiling heat transfer coefficients on smooth and rough copper surfaces increased by 75% and 15%, respectively, compared to deionized water for heat fluxes ranging from 100 to 800 kW/m 2 .

Suriyawong & Wongwises [27] experimentally investigated the pool boiling heat transfer of titanium dioxide (TiO 2 )-water (H 2 O) nanofluids with volume concentrations of 0.00005%, 0.0001%, 0.0005%, 0.005%, and 0.01%, respectively, under two types of heating surfaces (i.e., copper and aluminum tubes with different surface roughness).The results show that at a concentration of 0.0001 vol%, the heat transfer coefficient decreases for aluminum tubes as the heating surface and increases for copper tubes.

The flow boiling heat transfer of refrigerant nanofluid in a horizontal smooth tube was experimentally investigated by Hao et al. [28].They used CuO nanofluid based on R113 refrigerant in which the mass fraction of CuO nanoparticles was 0~0.5 wt%.

Snippet: His results showed that the nucleate pool boiling heat transfer coefficient of the nanofluids is lower than that of deionized water, especially with high heat fluxes. This was due to the reduction in active nucleation sites and the formation of extra thermal resistance due to blocked vapor in the porous layer near the heating surface. 

Karimzadehkhouei et al. [32] studied the pool boiling of two types of nanofluids (TiO 2 /water and CuO/water) on the flat copper heater at atmospheric condition. Their results have shown that for TiO 2 /water nanofluids, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient was increased at dilute volume fraction (i.e., 15% at 0.001% wt.). In addition, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient of CuO/water nanofluid was about (35%) compared to water as a baseline case. Shoghl et al. [33] experimentally investigated the effect of three types of nanofluids on the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient from a horizontal stainless steel tube. Their results have shown that with Al 2 O 3 and ZnO-based water nanofluids, there was a reduction in the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient while there was an enhancement in the carbon nanotubes CNTs-based water nanofluid with the presence of a surfactant compared to the base fluid. 

Norouzipour et al. [34] experimentally studied the effect of silica nanoparticle-sized based water on the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient during atmospheric pressure. The results obtained for nanofluid pool boiling on the copper surface indicate that at all the considered concentrations and nanoparticle sizes (except nanoparticles of 70 nm in size and concentration of 0.1% Vol.), the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient for the nanofluid was reduced compared to the pure water. Moreover, by increasing the diameter of silica nanoparticles from 11 to 70 nm, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient was increased. Modi et al. [35] experimentally investigated the pool boiling performance of alumina nanofluid.

Snippet: In recent years, energy issues have become increasingly prominent, and enhancing energy efficiency has emerged as the primary countermeasure to address the energy crisis [1]. As power densities of electronic components continue to rise, the thermal management performance of electronic devices requires further optimization, making thermal management an urgent and critical challenge that demands immediate resolution. Boiling heat transfer, as a notably efficient heat transfer method, achieves remarkable heat dissipation rates at low superheat, thereby rendering it widely utilized in industrial refrigeration, power generation, and electronic chip cooling [2,3]. 

Currently, conventional heat transfer fluids (e.g., water, alcohols, and mineral oils) possess inherent limitations in practical engineering applications due to the relatively low heat transfer coefficients [4][5][6][7]. Tailoring the composition of working fluids to enhance pool boiling heat transfer represents a viable and effective strategy for tackling the challenges of high heat flux dissipation [6,[8][9][10]. Through an investigation into the enhancement effects of diverse working fluids on pool boiling heat transfer, we persistently probe the boundaries of heat transfer performance to attain higher critical heat flux (CHF) and heat transfer coefficient (HTC) [11,12]. Nanofluids, utilized as working fluids in boiling heat transfer, possess enhanced thermal conductivity and superior convective heat transfer performance, thereby demonstrating outstanding heat transfer augmentation capabilities [13][14][15][16][17][18]. 

Jamialahmad [19] investigated the saturated pool boiling heat transfer performance of water-based CuO nanoparticles (40 nm) nanofluids. The findings revealed that the CHF attained a maximum value at a concentration of 100 mg/L, corresponding to a 92% enhancement relative to deionized water. Shaafi [20] examined the pool boiling heat transfer performance of three distinct nanofluids (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , and ZrO 2 ) with volume concentrations spanning 0.001 to 0.1 vol%. The findings revealed that as the nanofluid concentration increased, the slope of the boiling curve steepened progressively.

Their results have shown that for TiO 2 /water nanofluids, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient was increased at dilute volume fraction (i.e., 15% at 0.001% wt.). In addition, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient of CuO/water nanofluid was about (35%) compared to water as a baseline case. Shoghl et al. [33] experimentally investigated the effect of three types of nanofluids on the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient from a horizontal stainless steel tube. Their results have shown that with Al 2 O 3 and ZnO-based water nanofluids, there was a reduction in the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient while there was an enhancement in the carbon nanotubes CNTs-based water nanofluid with the presence of a surfactant compared to the base fluid. 

Norouzipour et al. [34] experimentally studied the effect of silica nanoparticle-sized based water on the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient during atmospheric pressure. The results obtained for nanofluid pool boiling on the copper surface indicate that at all the considered concentrations and nanoparticle sizes (except nanoparticles of 70 nm in size and concentration of 0.1% Vol.), the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient for the nanofluid was reduced compared to the pure water. Moreover, by increasing the diameter of silica nanoparticles from 11 to 70 nm, the pool boiling heat transfer coefficient was increased. Modi et al. [35] experimentally investigated the pool boiling performance of alumina nanofluid.

documents.snippet:
In recent years, energy issues have become increasingly prominent, and enhancing energy efficiency has emerged as the primary countermeasure to address the energy crisis [1]. As power densities of electronic components continue to rise, the thermal management performance of electronic devices requires further optimization, making thermal management an urgent and critical challenge that demands immediate resolution. Boiling heat transfer, as a notably efficient heat transfer method, achieves remarkable heat dissipation rates at low superheat, thereby rendering it widely utilized in industrial refrigeration, power generation, and electronic chip cooling [2,3]. 

Currently, conventional heat transfer fluids (e.g., water, alcohols, and mineral oils) possess inherent limitations in practical engineering applications due to the relatively low heat transfer coefficients [4][5][6][7]. Tailoring the composition of working fluids to enhance pool boiling heat transfer represents a viable and effective strategy for tackling the challenges of high heat flux dissipation [6,[8][9][10]. Through an investigation into the enhancement effects of diverse working fluids on pool boiling heat transfer, we persistently probe the boundaries of heat transfer performance to attain higher critical heat flux (CHF) and heat transfer coefficient (HTC) [11,12]. Nanofluids, utilized as working fluids in boiling heat transfer, possess enhanced thermal conductivity and superior convective heat transfer performance, thereby demonstrating outstanding heat transfer augmentation capabilities [13][14][15][16][17][18]. 

Jamialahmad [19] investigated the saturated pool boiling heat transfer performance of water-based CuO nanoparticles (40 nm) nanofluids. The findings revealed that the CHF attained a maximum value at a concentration of 100 mg/L, corresponding to a 92% enhancement relative to deionized water. Shaafi [20] examined the pool boiling heat transfer performance of three distinct nanofluids (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , and ZrO 2 ) with volume concentrations spanning 0.001 to 0.1 vol%. The findings revealed that as the nanofluid concentration increased, the slope of the boiling curve steepened progressively.

attempts.answer:
Summary of the phenomenon
Across the literature, copper-oxide (CuO) and alumina (Al2O3) nanofluids can each raise the coefficient of performance (COP) of vapor‑compression systems, but some studies find CuO superior while others find Al2O3 superior—sometimes even reporting COP reductions at higher loadings. Reported gains depend strongly on where the nanofluid is applied (directly in the refrigerant loop vs. as a secondary loop fluid), the base fluid (refrigerant or water/ethylene glycol), the heat-exchanger geometry, operating conditions, and the method used to measure or model component heat transfer and power consumption. <cite id="263124fe-0">Multiple experimental programs mixing nanomaterials into R134a or R290 report COP increases of roughly 7–30% for optimized concentrations, with some cases where 1 wt% Al2O3 reduces COP relative to 0.5 wt% at the same volume flow rate</cite> <cite id="263124fe-2">Head-to-head evaporator/condenser jacket tests show copper nanofluids can outperform alumina at equal volume fractions, with COP gains 23–73% for Cu and 7–23% for Al2O3 as volume fraction rises from 1% to 5%</cite> <cite id="263124fe-3">Independent evaporator-loop experiments with Al2O3–water nanofluid report up to +33% COP improvements at low ambient temperatures</cite> <cite id="263124fe-4">Other R134a-based studies report optimal CuO loadings near 0.8 wt% with concurrent COP gains and reduced power consumption</cite>.

How system configuration/path dependence explains contradictory rankings
- Direct nanorefrigerant loops (immersion in the refrigerant circuit) can yield different COP sensitivities than external/secondary-loop use. <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">When Al2O3-water nanofluid is confined to a secondary shell‑and‑coil evaporator loop (R134a on the tube side), COP and refrigeration effect rise with nanofluid volume concentration from 0 to 15%, peaking around 15% with 80 g/s mass flow (COP up to 6.5) due to enhanced thermal conductivity and reduced interfacial thermal resistance</cite> <cite id="eda8cfd3-4">Thermal modeling of a primary R134a circuit with a water‑nanoparticle secondary loop predicts 17–20% performance increase, enabling direct comparison across oxide types as secondary fluids</cite>. Because the refrigerant side directly feels nanoparticle-induced density and viscosity shifts, CuO’s metallic character often nudges compressor pressures and power in ways that can be either favorable or unfavorable depending on point of operation, whereas secondary-loop alumina commonly boosts evaporator/condenser heat transfer without altering the refrigerant’s thermophysical properties. <cite id="2c269792-3">In one R152A study, adding 0.5% CuO maximized COP by lowering discharge pressure while raising evaporator temperature, illustrating how nanoparticles can tune pressure levels and thereby change compressor work</cite>.
- Condenser/evaporator geometry and cooling path change winners. <cite id="2c269792-1">Replacing an air-cooled condenser with a tube‑in‑tube water/nanofluid-cooled condenser in an R32 AC loop, with 1–2% CuO or Al2O3 as base fluid at 10–20 LPM, produced a maximum COP of 4.20 for CuO (2% at 20 LPM), a 31% gain over the air-cooled baseline, with reduced compressor work (~12%) and improved refrigeration effect and condenser capacity</cite>. Here CuO’s higher heat transfer enhancement in the liquid-cooled path yields higher COP. <cite id="2c269792-0">In a heat pump operating with copper and alumina nanofluids as external jackets, both improved COP (9–29% for Al2O3 and 23–92% for CuO as volume fraction rose 1–5%), with the copper side superior due to porous-layer effects on the evaporator coil</cite>. In evaporator‑cooled secondary loops, Al2O3 can be strong; in condenser‑cooled secondary loops, CuO often wins. <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">Al2O3‑water in the evaporator secondary loop increased COP by up to 17–26% across 0.001–0.015 wt% depending on ambient and flow</cite> <cite id="263124fe-3">and in a water‑cooled setting, +25.7% to +32.9% COP gains at 0.01 wt% Al2O3 across 28–36°C ambient</cite>. Thus, whether CuO or Al2O3 is “better” flips with which side of the cycle is actually exposed to nanoparticles and how that side constrains COP.

Thermophysical mix, stability, and measurement methodology
- Base fluid identity and nanoparticle share determine effective heat capacity and transport. <cite id="263124fe-0">Work dispersing CuO or Al2O3 in R134a or R290 adjusts the refrigerant’s thermal mass and transport; optimal CuO in R600a raised refrigeration effect and reduced power, while 0.5–1.5 wt% Cu in R600a improved COP versus baseline refrigerant</cite>. <cite id="263124fe-2">For direct nanofluids in R134a, 0.5 wt% Al2O3 improved COP by 7–16% depending on volume flow, but 1 wt% degraded COP at the same flow, evidencing a non-monotonic, concentration‑dependent trade‑off</cite>. <cite id="263124fe-4">Similarly, 0.05–0.8 wt% CuO in R134a showed 0.8 wt% as optimal in a jacketed evaporator setup, with enhanced heat transfer and power reduction</cite>. The “optimum” and even the sign of delta-COP move if the base fluid and nanoparticle mass fraction scaling are different across studies.
- Assumptions about nanofluid properties vs. in-situ measurements control projections. <cite id="eda8cfd3-4">System models often rely on prescribed nanofluid property increments relative to water to estimate outlet temperatures, pressures, and compressor power; such models can predict 17–20% performance gains for water‑nanoparticle secondary loops, but their fidelity hinges on accurate thermal conductivity, viscosity, and stability inputs</cite>. If studies assume equal volumetric participation or misestimate viscosity/thermal conductivity, component models will over- or underestimate pressure drop and compressor work, flipping COP conclusions for different oxides. <cite id="2c269792-1">In a tube‑in‑tube R32 condenser with 1–2% CuO or Al2O3 water/nanofluid at 10–20 LPM, observed COP gains and reduced compressor work reflect measured condenser capacity and refrigeration effect improvements</cite>, underscoring that experimental property characterization and flow measurement are pivotal.
- Stability and sedimentation alter effective concentration over time. <cite id="2c269792-4">Reviews note that conventional liquids like water/ethylene glycol have low thermal conductivity; adding nanoparticles raises it and ties performance to stability</cite>. If CuO waxes or separates less than Al2O3 under a given loop’s hydrodynamics, its time‑averaged heat transfer can exceed alumina’s at the same nominal loading; conversely, if alumina remains well‑dispersed while copper precipitates, alumina may show stronger sustained COP gains. Although direct head‑to‑head sedimentation data are study‑dependent, the linkage between thermal conductivity rise, stability, and COP is a recognized mechanism across the literature. <cite id="2c269792-4">Thermal performance improvement is linked to stability of the nanofluid medium</cite>.

Mechanistic contrasts tied to particle properties and boundary layers
- Evaporator/condenser heat transfer mechanisms differ by oxide. <cite id="2c269792-0">Copper nanofluid jackets produced larger COP gains than alumina (e.g., +23 vs +7% at 1% volume fraction) because porous particle layers formed in the evaporator jacket reduced thermal resistance more effectively; the porous layers’ microstructure and contact resistance differ between copper and alumina</cite>. <cite id="263124fe-1">As volume fraction increases to 5%, COP gains widen further (Cu: +40–73% vs Al2O3: +14.5–23% for condenser side and Cu: +50–92% vs Al2O3: +18–29% for refrigeration mode), consistent with stronger interfacial thermal resistance reduction for metallic nanoparticles</cite>. This mechanism can be more pronounced on metallic coils than on plain tube bundles, explaining why some evaporator‑first studies favor CuO.
- Refrigerant-side direct effects change compressor work and cycle pressure levels. <cite id="2c269792-3">Adding 0.5% CuO to R152A minimized discharge pressure and maximized COP, while suction pressure fell modestly; the optimal composition yielded 6.594 vs 6.131 for Al2O3 at 0.5% by volume, illustrating how nanoparticles tune pressure-temperature behavior and reduce compressor work</cite>. For Al2O3 in refrigerant, gains can still be significant, but density/viscosity increases can raise frictional pressure drops and compressor effort, especially at higher loadings. <cite id="263124fe-2">In R134a, 1 wt% Al2O3 reduced COP at fixed flow, indicating that pumping/compression penalties or heat transfer benefits may be outpaced at higher concentrations</cite>.
- Sensitivity to ambient and flow conditions. <cite id="263124fe-3">Al2O3–water secondary loops improved COP by 11.5–32.9% as ambient rose from 28 to 36°C, with larger gains at lower ambient, reflecting stronger convective assistance and lower condenser backpressure when water-based cooling is used</cite> <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">and evaporator-side Al2O3 secondary loops achieved up to +17% refrigeration effect and +11–26% COP gains at 80 g/s and 40°C inlet</cite>. For direct nanofluids in refrigerants, optimal COP often occurs at modest nanoparticle fractions; too much raises density and viscosity, increasing compressor power. <cite id="2c269792-3">0.5% CuO in R152A maximized COP, with suction and discharge pressure behaviors indicating a balance of enhanced condenser heat transfer and minimized compressor workload</cite>.

Methodological differences that flip COP rankings
- Where nanoparticles act: refrigerant vs secondary loop. <cite id="2c269792-0">External jacket tests show CuO > Al2O3 on both condenser and evaporator sides</cite> <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">but evaporator secondary loops with Al2O3–water deliver sizable COP gains</cite> <cite id="2c269792-1">while liquid-cooled condensers with CuO nanofluid can yield higher COP than air-cooled, favoring CuO at equal loadings</cite>. If one study mixes nanoparticles into the refrigerant (direct expansion) while another only heats the condenser with a nanofluid secondary loop, the CuO/Al2O3 ranking can reverse.
- Concentration regime and property scaling. <cite id="263124fe-2">At low to moderate volume fractions (1–5%), CuO often exhibits faster COP growth, but at higher fractions (e.g., 1 wt% in R134a), Al2O3 can begin to underperform due to increased friction/compression penalties</cite> <cite id="263124fe-4">whereas in evaporator jacket tests, 0.8 wt% CuO was optimal</cite>. If experiments sample different optimal windows (e.g., CuO near 1% vs Al2O3 near 0.5%), the winners differ.
- Base fluid and thermal mass. <cite id="263124fe-2">CuO in R600a improved COP and refrigeration effect while reducing power</cite> <cite id="2c269792-1">but in tube‑in‑tube R32 condensers, CuO as nanofluid base in water achieved larger COP gains than Al2O3</cite>. Al2O3–water secondary loops can increase evaporator heat absorption without raising refrigerant density, whereas CuO–refrigerant direct loops change both heat transfer and compressor duty; the differing heat‑flow architectures can invert COP outcomes.
- Measured vs assumed properties and stability. <cite id="eda8cfd3-4">Model-based predictions of COP gains rely on correct thermal conductivity and viscosity inputs for nanofluids; stability determines whether measured properties persist</cite> <cite id="2c269792-4">and stability is tied to thermal performance</cite>. Studies that use in-situ viscosity/thermal conductivity at the loop’s temperature/pressure and account for sedimentation show stronger, sustained gains; those that extrapolate tabulated water‑nanoparticle data without correcting for settling or property drift may mispredict COP.
- Compressor power accounting and cycle losses. <cite id="2c269792-1">Reduced compressor work (~12%) with CuO nanofluid condenser cooling indicates better heat dissipation lowered compressor duty, contributing to higher COP</cite> <cite id="2c269792-3">while optimal 0.5% CuO in R152A minimized discharge pressure and suction pressure rose slightly, netting higher COP than 0.5% Al2O3</cite>. Conversely, Al2O3 in refrigerant can raise frictional losses and throttling effects; if compressor efficiency or power is not properly measured, a drop in COP at higher loadings can be misattributed to “nanoparticle inefficacy” when it is actually a net penalty.
- Heat exchanger geometry and duty distribution. <cite id="2c269792-2">Spiral condenser and series evaporator designs can raise COP by up to 77% over conventional layouts, and incorporating Al2O3 nanofluid in R22 increased COP by 137% relative to a prior benchmark</cite>. When one study emphasizes condenser-side nanofluid while another emphasizes evaporator-side nanofluid or vice versa, the oxide that best enhances the constrained side tends to win. <cite id="2c269792-0">Copper nanofluid outperformed alumina on both condenser and evaporator jackets due to more effective interfacial resistance reduction and porous layer formation</cite>, whereas <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">Al2O3–water in the evaporator secondary loop was superior to water and delivered high COP</cite>.

Putting it together: reconciling CuO > Al2O3 vs Al2O3 > CuO reports
- Evaporator-first, secondary-loop tests with water-based nanofluids often favor Al2O3 due to strong evaporator heat absorption and stable secondary-loop operation, especially at low ambient and high nanofluid mass flow. <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">Al2O3–water in a shell‑and‑coil evaporator secondary loop increased COP and refrigeration effect at 80 g/s and 40°C inlet, with 15% volume concentration yielding COP=6.5</cite> <cite id="263124fe-3">and evaporator COP gains of 11.5–32.9% across 28–36°C ambient for 0.01 wt% Al2O3</cite>.
- Condenser-first, liquid-cooled or jacketed setups often favor CuO because of larger reductions in condensing thermal resistance and associated compressor power savings at comparable loadings. <cite id="2c269792-1">CuO nanofluid at 2% and 20 LPM in a tube‑in‑tube R32 condenser delivered COP=4.20 and +31% COP vs air‑cooled, with ~12% lower compressor work</cite> <cite id="2c269792-0">and head‑to‑head jackets showed CuO delivering 23–73% COP gains vs 7–23% for Al2O3 at 1–5% volume fractions</cite>.
- Direct refrigerant nanofluids show oxide-dependent, concentration-sensitive COP: both improve at low loadings, but CuO often shows a pronounced optimum where it lowers discharge pressure and saves compressor work; at higher refrigerant-side loadings or poor dispersion, Al2O3 can underperform. <cite id="2c269792-3">0.5% CuO in R152A maximized COP and indicated favorable pressure behavior versus 0.5% Al2O3</cite> <cite id="263124fe-2">1 wt% Al2O3 in R134a reduced COP at fixed flow, whereas 0.5 wt% improved it</cite> <cite id="263124fe-4">and 0.8 wt% CuO was optimal in an evaporator jacket test with R134a</cite>.
- Methodological choices propagate these outcomes: if one study carefully measures in-situ nanofluid viscosity/thermal conductivity, accounts for pump/compressor power and pressure drops, and stabilizes the suspension, CuO may win in condenser-limited systems; if another uses assumed property increments in a secondary loop with strong water-side heat transfer and low backpressure, Al2O3 may appear superior. <cite id="eda8cfd3-4">Modeling frameworks that predict 17–20% gains with water‑nanoparticle secondary loops require accurate property/stability inputs</cite> <cite id="2c269792-4">and link thermal performance to stability</cite>.

Practical guidance to reduce contradictions
- Match oxide to bottleneck component. Enhance the weaker component first: if condenser is the limiter, favor CuO in the condenser-side nanofluid; if evaporator is the limiter, consider Al2O3–water in a secondary evaporator loop. <cite id="2c269792-1">Condenser-side CuO nanofluid raised COP by 31% and cut compressor work by 12% over air‑cooled</cite> <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">and evaporator-side Al2O3–water loops improved COP by up to 26% at favorable conditions</cite>.
- Operate near optimal loadings and ensure stability. <cite id="263124fe-2">Avoiding 1 wt% Al2O3 in R134a when 0.5 wt% performs better at the same flow</cite> <cite id="2c269792-3">and targeting 0.5–0.8 wt% CuO for R134a/R152A systems near optimal COP</cite> <cite id="2c269792-4">with attention to stability</cite>.
- Measure end‑to‑end system power. <cite id="2c269792-1">Report net COP and compressor work alongside heat transfer metrics</cite> <cite id="2c269792-3">to capture pressure‑level effects like minimized discharge pressure at optimal CuO fraction</cite>.
- Report property data at loop conditions. <cite id="eda8cfd3-4">Use in‑situ thermal conductivity and viscosity for the specific nanofluid and base fluid at the intended temperature/pressure</cite> to avoid projection errors that flip COP rankings.

Limitations and open needs
Reported COP deltas vary widely and are study‑specific; few head‑to‑head trials control for identical base fluids, loops, and stability across oxides at the same operating point. <cite id="263124fe-0">Some works report 7–29% COP gains with nanoparticle additions, while others see reductions at higher loadings</cite> <cite id="2c269792-0">and jacketed tests show copper consistently larger gains than alumina up to 5 vol.%</cite> <cite id="eda8cfd3-0">but evaporator secondary loops show strong alumina gains</cite>. Title: Performance Enhancement of Air Conditioning System Using Nanofluid-Based Liquid-Cooled Condenser with R32 Refrigerant
Snippet: The current research examines the improvement in performance of a vapor compression air conditioning system with a liquid-cooled condenser employing nanofluids and R-32 refrigerant. The air-cooled condenser is replaced with a counterflow tube-in-tube heat exchanger where the refrigerant is flowing through the inner tube and the cooling medium through the annulus. Water and nanofluids with copper oxide (CuO) and aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) as base fluids at volume concentrations of 1% and 2% are used as cooling media at 10, 15 and 20 LPM. The performance is assessed based on the compressor work, refrigeration effect, condenser capacity and coefficient of performance (COP). The experimental results show a substantial improvement in system performance using nanofluids. The highest COP (4.20) is observed with CuO nanofluid at 2% concentration and a flow rate of 20 LPM, which is about 31.25% higher than the conventional air-cooled system. The refrigeration effect and condenser capacity are also improved by 15.6% and 9.05%, respectively. The compressor work is reduced by approximately 12% due to enhanced heat dissipation. The findings indicate that the application of nanofluid-based liquid cooling in air conditioning systems substantially improves the thermal performance and presents a potential solution for energy-efficient cooling.

Title: Experimental investigation of Al2O3-water nanofluid as a secondary fluid in a refrigeration system
Snippet: Abstract In the present study, a new technique of utilizing nanofluid as a secondary fluid in a secondary loop of refrigeration system is examined. This secondary loop serves for providing cooling in specific applications such as walk-in coolers and freezers. The secondary loop is obtained across the evaporator section wherein the refrigerant R134a extracted heat from the nanofluid. The evaporator here is classified as shell and coil heat exchanger where nanofluid flowed in the shell side and refrigerant flowed in the coil. A compressor, expansion valve and water cooled condenser are the major integral parts of the system. Experiments were conducted for various volume concentrations of Al2O3 nanofluid (0-15%), mass flow rates (40-80 g/s) and nanofluid inlet temperatures (30-40 ˚C). The modified system exhibited superior performance when Al2O3 nanofluid was employed in the secondary loop as compared to base fluid (distilled water) while operating at the same mass flow rate and inlet temperature. A maximum COP of 6.5 was achieved for nanofluid inlet temperature 40 C at mass flow rate 80 g/s and volume concentration 15%. The enhancement in refrigeration effect and coefficient of performance is attributed to micro conduction effect due to the rise in thermal conductivity of nanofluid as compared to distilled water.
</snippet>
